meta.note: Rounds with a "daily" id take their question and right answer from data/daily-questions.json, so both features agree. "q" and "right" here are only used if that question is missing.

rounds.q: What's one thing you're really good at?
wrong: Are you better than the other people applying?
Can you list all of your skills?
rounds.why: They don't need a list or a comparison. They want one real strength they can believe.
rounds.tip: Name one strength, then tell a quick story that shows it.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time something didn't go the way you planned.
wrong: Do things usually go wrong for you?
Who was to blame when it went wrong?
rounds.why: It's not about the problem or whose fault it was. It's about what you did next.
rounds.tip: Spend one sentence on what went wrong and most of your answer on how you handled it.

rounds.q: How do you handle having a lot to do at once?
wrong: Are you too busy to take this on?
Do you like being busy?
rounds.why: They're not checking your schedule or your feelings about it. They want to know you have a way to cope.
rounds.tip: Describe your method, like a list or doing the closest deadline first, and a busy week when it worked.

rounds.q: How would your friends describe you?
wrong: Are you popular?
Do you have a lot of friends?
rounds.why: The number of friends doesn't matter. It's a way to hear what you're like from someone else's view.
rounds.tip: Pick one quality a friend would really say, and add a quick example of it.

rounds.q: What's something you're working on getting better at?
wrong: What's the worst thing about you?
Is there a reason we shouldn't pick you?
rounds.why: It's not a trap. They want honesty plus proof you're growing.
rounds.tip: Choose a real but not deal-breaking weakness, then say what you're doing about it.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you worked with a group.
wrong: Do you prefer working alone or in groups?
What was the group project about?
rounds.why: The topic of the project barely matters. They're picturing you on their team.
rounds.tip: Say what you did to help the group, not just what the group did.

rounds.q: Tell me about a mistake you made and what you did next.
wrong: How many mistakes do you usually make?
Can you prove you never mess up?
rounds.why: Everyone makes mistakes. They're looking for honesty and what you did about it.
rounds.tip: Own it in one line, then say how you fixed it and what you do differently now.

rounds.q: What made you interested in applying?
wrong: How did you hear about us?
Do you need this for a school requirement?
rounds.why: They want to know you chose them on purpose.
rounds.tip: Give one specific reason that's about this place, not any place.

rounds.q: What do you do when you feel nervous?
wrong: Are you nervous right now?
Is something wrong with how you handle stress?
rounds.why: Being nervous is normal. They want to see you have a way to steady yourself.
rounds.tip: Share one thing that works for you and a time you used it.

rounds.q: What would you ask to find out if this is a good fit for you?
wrong: Do you have any complaints about us?
Are you planning to apply somewhere else?
rounds.why: It's an invitation to show you're thinking about the fit from your side too.
rounds.tip: Ask about something that matters to you, like how people learn or what a normal day is like.

rounds.q: What makes you a good teammate?
wrong: Have you played on a sports team?
Do people like you?
rounds.why: It doesn't have to be sports, and being liked isn't the point. They want a specific way you help a team.
rounds.tip: Name one thing you do for a team, and show it with a short example.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone.
wrong: Do you argue a lot?
Were you right in the end?
rounds.why: Who won doesn't matter much. What matters is how you handled it.
rounds.tip: Show that you listened, explained calmly, and found a fair way to settle it.

rounds.q: What's your biggest weakness?
wrong: What's the reason we should say no?
Can you turn a strength into a weakness?
rounds.why: They're checking honesty and self-awareness. A disguised brag like 'I'm a perfectionist' misses it.
rounds.tip: Name something real, keep it small, and say how you're working on it.

rounds.q: Why should we pick you?
wrong: Why are you better than everyone else?
How badly do you want this?
rounds.why: It's not about beating others or how much you want it. It's about the match between you and them.
rounds.tip: Link one or two things you're good at to what they need, with a quick example.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you got feedback you didn't like.
wrong: Who has criticized you before?
Do you get in trouble a lot?
rounds.why: They're not digging for trouble. They want to know you can hear criticism and get better.
rounds.tip: Say what the feedback was, how it felt honestly, and what you changed because of it.

rounds.q: What would you do if you realized you'd made a mistake no one else noticed?
wrong: Are you good at hiding mistakes?
Do you pay close attention to details?
rounds.why: It's a question about honesty, not about attention to detail.
rounds.tip: Say you'd point it out and help fix it, and give a time you did something like that if you can.

rounds.q: What would you do if you didn't understand what you were asked to do?
wrong: Do you have trouble understanding instructions?
Are you smart enough for this?
rounds.why: They're not testing how smart you are. They want to know you won't guess and get it wrong.
rounds.tip: Say you'd ask a clear question, and maybe repeat back what you heard to check.

rounds.q: What's one thing you want me to remember about you?
wrong: What's your name again?
Can you repeat your whole answer from earlier?
rounds.why: They want a short, clear takeaway, not a full recap.
rounds.tip: Pick one quality or story from the interview and say it in a sentence or two.

rounds.q: What's your availability?
rounds.right: Can we actually schedule you when we need people?
wrong: How busy is your social life?
Will you work any hours we give you, no matter what?
rounds.why: They need to build a schedule. Clear and honest beats saying 'whenever'.
rounds.tip: Give the days and times you can work, and mention limits like sports or school up front.

rounds.q: Why do you want to work here?
rounds.right: Do you want this job, or just any job?
wrong: How much do you know about our company history?
Do you need the money?
rounds.why: Most people need the money, and they know that. They want a reason this place fits you.
rounds.tip: Mention something you know or like about the place, and what you hope to learn there.

rounds.q: What would you do if a customer was rude to you?
rounds.right: Will you stay calm and respectful, and get help if you need it?
wrong: Have you had bad customers before?
Would you stand up for yourself?
rounds.why: They're picturing you at the counter on a bad day. Staying calm protects the customer and you.
rounds.tip: Say you'd listen, stay polite, try to fix it, and get a manager if it goes beyond you.

rounds.q: Have you ever had a job before?
rounds.right: Have you done anything that shows you'd be responsible at work?
wrong: Do you have a work history we can check?
Is this your first job, so we can pay you less?
rounds.why: For a first job, they don't expect work history. Babysitting, chores and clubs all count.
rounds.tip: If it's your first job, say so, then point to something where people counted on you.

rounds.q: How would you handle a really busy shift?
rounds.right: Will you stay focused and keep up when it gets hectic?
wrong: Do you like busy places?
Can you work faster than everyone else?
rounds.why: Speed isn't everything. They want someone who stays steady and helps the team keep up.
rounds.tip: Talk about staying calm, doing one thing at a time, and asking teammates for help if needed.

rounds.q: What would you do if you finished your tasks early?
rounds.right: Will you look for more to do, or stand around?
wrong: Do you work too fast and make mistakes?
Would you like to go home early?
rounds.why: They're checking if you'll do more than the minimum.
rounds.tip: Say you'd ask what else needs doing, or find something obvious like restocking or cleaning.

rounds.q: Why are you interested in this school?
rounds.right: Do you know what makes us different, and why it matters to you?
wrong: How high is this school on your list?
Did your parents tell you to apply?
rounds.why: General praise fits every school. They want to know you looked at this one.
rounds.tip: Name one or two things only this school has, and connect them to what you want to do.

rounds.q: What do you want to study?
rounds.right: What are you curious about, and have you thought about it?
wrong: Have you already chosen your career?
Will you pick a major that's hard to get into?
rounds.why: Lots of students are undecided. They care more about curiosity than a final answer.
rounds.tip: If you're undecided, say so, then share what you're drawn to and why.

rounds.q: How would you contribute to our campus?
rounds.right: What would you add to the community here?
wrong: How many clubs will you join?
Will you bring in money or awards?
rounds.why: They're picturing you on campus. It's about what you'd add, not how many things you'd sign up for.
rounds.tip: Point to something you've already done or started, and how it could carry over to campus.

rounds.q: Tell me about a class that challenged you.
rounds.right: How do you handle hard work you can't do easily?
wrong: Which teacher do you not like?
Are your grades good enough?
rounds.why: Grades are already in your application. They want to see how you work through something hard.
rounds.tip: Name the class, what was hard, what you did about it, and how it turned out.

rounds.q: What do you do outside of school?
rounds.right: Who are you beyond your grades?
wrong: Do you have enough activities on your application?
Do you spend too much time on hobbies?
rounds.why: It's not a count of activities. Family duties, jobs and hobbies all show who you are.
rounds.tip: Pick one or two things you care about and add a detail that makes them yours.

rounds.q: Is there anything else you'd like us to know?
rounds.right: Is there something important we haven't asked about?
wrong: Do you want to end the interview now?
Can you repeat your strongest point?
rounds.why: It's an open door to share context your application doesn't show.
rounds.tip: If there's something real, like a hard year or a big responsibility, share it briefly. If not, thank them and add one last reason you'd fit.
